title: Anglo-Zulu War
wiki_lead:
The Anglo-Zulu War, or simply the Zulu War, was fought in present-day South Africa from January to early July 1879 between forces of the British Empire and the Zulu Kingdom. Two famous battles of the war were the Zulu victory at Isandlwana and the British defence at Rorke's Drift.
Following the passing of the British North America Act 1867 forming a federation in Canada, Lord Carnarvon thought that a similar political effort, coupled with military campaigns, might lead to a ruling white minority over a black majority in South Africa. This would yield a large pool of cheap labour for the British sugar plantations and mines, and was intended to bring the African Kingdoms, tribal areas, and Boer republics into South Africa.
In 1877, Sir Bartle Frere was appointed as British High Commissioner for Southern Africa to effect such plans.  Among the obstacles were the armed independent states of the South African Republic and the Zulu Kingdom.
Frere, on his own initiative, sent a provocative ultimatum on 11 December 1878 to Zulu King Cetshwayo.  Upon its rejection, he ordered Lord Chelmsford to invade Zululand. The war had several particularly bloody battles, including an opening victory for the Zulu at the Battle of Isandlwana, followed by the defence of Rorke's Drift by a small British Garrison from an attack by a large Zulu force. However, the British eventually gained the upper hand at Kambula, before taking the Zulu capital of Ulundi. The British eventually won the war, ending Zulu dominance of the region. The British Empire made the Zulu Kingdom a protectorate and later annexed it in 1887.

Background


Zulu Kingdom

The Zulu Kingdom grew from a small tribe to a large regional power under Shaka in the 1810s, his successors Dingane and Mpande got two powerful new neigbours the Boers and the British Empire. After a civil war in the 1850s Mpande's son Cetshwayo became the heir and de facto ruler.

In spite of his dislike for their activities, Cetshwayo permitted European missionaries in Zululand. Though he did not harm or persecute the missionaries themselves, several converts were killed. The missionaries, for their part, were a source of hostile reports. While numerous Zulus of rival factions fled into Natal and some of the surrounding areas, Cetshwayo continued and maintained the peaceful relations with the Natal colonists that had prevailed for decades. 
After Mpande died of old age in 1872 Cetshwayo was acclaimed king by his izinduna in 1873  and had a coronation a month later where Shepstone as Natal's Secretary for Native Affairs proclaimed a set of 'coronation laws,' that challenged traditional Zulu social rites. 
As ruler, Cetshwayo set about reviving the military methods of his uncle Shaka as far as possible. He formed new age-set regiments and even succeeded in equipping his regiments with a few antiquated muskets and other outdated firearms. Most Zulu warriors were armed with an iklwa (the Zulu refinement of the assegai thrusting spear) and a shield made of cowhide. The Zulu army drilled in the personal and tactical use and coordination of this weapons system. While some Zulus also had firearms, their marksmanship training was poor and the quality and supply of their powder and shot was dreadful. The Zulu attitude towards firearms was summarized: "The generality of Zulu warriors, however, would not have firearms – the arms of a coward, as they said, for they enable the poltroon to kill the brave without awaiting his attack."


Boers
Although the Boers were originally from the Dutch Cape Colony many were gradually leaving the now British colony in the Great Trek, partly to escape British Rule but also for more land - and set up a number of Boer republics including the Utrecht Republic in an area that had been depopulated after the expulsion of the Hlubi.

grok_lead: The Anglo-Zulu War was a colonial war of British imperial expansion fought against the independent Zulu Kingdom from January to August 1879 in southeastern Africa, now KwaZulu-Natal province, South Africa. Triggered by High Commissioner Sir Henry Bartle Frere's ultimatum on 11 December 1878âdemanding Zulu disarmament, border adjustments, and submission to British arbitration, which King Cetshwayo kaMpande rejected as infringing Zulu sovereigntyâthe conflict arose from Britain's confederation policy to consolidate control over southern African polities amid diamond discoveries and fears of Zulu military power destabilizing settler economies. Frere, acting without explicit London approval despite Prime Minister Disraeli's reluctance for war, fabricated pretexts like alleged Zulu border raids to justify invasion, reflecting causal drivers of resource extraction and administrative hegemony rather than defensive necessity. British forces under Lieutenant-General Lord Chelmsford invaded Zululand in three columns on 11 January 1879, underestimating Zulu impis' mobility and short stabbing assegai tactics honed under Shaka's mfecane legacy. The war's defining early shock was the Zulu annihilation of 1,329 British and colonial troops at Isandlwana on 22 January, where 20,000 warriors under Ntshingwayo kaMahole exploited divided British lines and ammunition shortages, killing the largest single loss of British regulars in any colonial campaign. This humiliation spurred immediate Zulu assaults on British bases, but 150 defenders at Rorke's Drift repelled 4,000 attackers over 12 hours on 22â23 January, earning 11 Victoria Crosses amid brutal close-quarters fighting that highlighted British Martini-Henry rifle fire's edge despite Zulu numerical superiority. Chelmsford's reinforcements and tactical shifts culminated in the decisive square-formation victory at Ulundi on 4 July, where 5,000 British troops routed Cetshwayo's last field army of 15,000â20,000, killing thousands and burning the royal kraal, after which Cetshwayo fled and was captured on 28 August. The British triumph dismantled the Zulu monarchy's central authority, partitioning Zululand into 13 chieftaincies under pro-British appointees, imposing hut taxes to extract labor for Natal plantations, and exiling Cetshwayo until his brief 1883 restoration amid civil unrest, which further fragmented the kingdom before full Natal annexation in 1887. Controversies included Chelmsford's scapegoating subordinates for Isandlwana âignoring his own force-splitting errorsâand Frere's recall for provoking avoidable hostilities, underscoring how imperial overreach exposed logistical vulnerabilities against adaptive indigenous resistance, though superior firepower and reserves ensured conquest. The war's legacy endures in military historiography for tactical lessons, with Zulu cohesion yielding to British divide-and-rule, enabling unchecked resource dominance in the subcontinent.
